items.title: Directories on the Hook: CMS Proposes New Medicare Advantage Directory Rules - Epstein Becker Green
items.reason: CMS regulatory enforcement action targeting Medicare Advantage payer operations (directory accuracy) directly impacts payer compliance obligations and potential sanctions, affecting revenue-cycle workflows around network management.
items.summary: CMS has proposed new regulatory rules governing Medicare Advantage plan directories, establishing stricter requirements for payer accuracy and maintenance of provider network information. The proposed rules represent a regulatory enforcement mechanism that will hold MA plans accountable for directory deficiencies, with non-compliance potentially triggering CMS sanctions. Revenue-cycle teams are affected because inaccurate directories create claim denials, payment delays, and provider network disputes; compliance requires coordinating with payers on directory updates and managing the operational burden of verification requirements. This matters for revenue-cycle teams as CMS enforcement against payers for directory failures can reduce claim denials attributable to network status mismatches and strengthen leverage in appealing previously denied claims.

items.title: UnitedHealthcare eliminates prior authorization requirements on 2K pediatric services
items.reason: This represents a significant payer policy change affecting prior authorization practices, which directly impacts revenue-cycle operations; while not litigation/enforcement per se, it reflects the type of payer policy shift that often results from or relates to regulatory pressure and enforcement actions against payers over claims-denial practices.
items.summary: UnitedHealthcare announced it will eliminate prior authorization requirements for more than 2,000 pediatric service codes effective December 1. This policy change removes administrative barriers that revenue-cycle teams currently navigate when processing pediatric claims, reducing claim denials and rework. The elimination of prior-auth requirements on this scale reflects broader industry pressure around claims-denial practices and streamlines the authorization process for a high-volume service category, potentially improving claim acceptance rates and cash flow for pediatric providers.
